title: Everybody Thinks, Everybody Learns: If We Plan for It
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: Starting from David Perkins's claim that learning is a consequence of thinking, the author argues that teachers must plan deliberately for every student to think rather than hope it happens. He lists participation techniques, including cold calling, choral response, I Say You Say, turn and talk, think-pair-share, mini-whiteboards and everybody writes, and explains when in a lesson each fits. He describes an Everybody Thinks planning template that moves from the lesson objective, to a bank of prompts, to sequencing within an explicit-instruction lesson, to combining techniques. He adds Project Zero thinking routines for depth, and stresses that the techniques work only when taught, modelled and held to as routines, followed by reflection after each lesson.
points: No thinking means no learning, so the thinking of every student has to be designed into the lesson.
Each participation technique has a best moment in a lesson, such as cold calling for guided practice and choral response for vocabulary and facts.
A template links lesson objective, prompt bank and lesson sequence so the techniques are not dropped in at random.
Combining techniques, for example everybody writes then think-pair-share then cold call, multiplies thinking.
Techniques only become routines if taught from day one, modelled and enforced consistently with warm strictness.
quotes: Based on this claim, which is supported by decades of research showing the correlation between thinking and learning, to ensure every student learns, then we must first ensure everybody thinks. In other words, no thinking equals no learning.
Students must construct their own knowledge and understanding. It cannot be absorbed through osmosis just by listening.

Thinking has to be intentionally planned for and orchestrated in the same way that presenting new content is during a lesson. This is especially true if your objective is for everybody to think. And it should be.
The kids know when it’s not. They have a sixth sense of sorts for sniffing out a process that the teacher has not fully thought through and is simply ad-libbing on the fly.
Next comes the most important step: when to leverage these strategies during instruction. The timing makes all the difference.
It’s only a procedure if the procedure is followed. It’s only a routine if we do it with as little variation as possible each time.
